title: The Divinity Verses Examined One by One
subtitle: John 1:1, 8:58, 10:30, 20:28, Philippians 2:6-8, Colossians 2:9, and Titus 2:13 — the Greek grammar, the Trinitarian case, and the unitarian case, side by side
summary: Christians cite a small group of New Testament passages as evidence that Jesus is divine. Each deserves its strongest reading. None should be isolated from Jesus's repeated prayers, his distinction between himself and God, or his identification of the Father as the only true God. Islam reads the exalted language as honor given to God's Messiah, not permission to worship him.

seo.metaTitle: The Divinity Verses Examined One by One: John 1:1 to Titus 2:13
seo.metaDescription: Examine the New Testament verses most often cited for Jesus's divinity, the strongest Christian readings, Jesus's own words about God, and the Quranic conclusion.

sections.title: Do the New Testament's Divinity Verses Prove That Jesus Is God?
sections.body: Christians cite several New Testament passages as evidence that Jesus is God. Some are grammatically strong within the theology of their authors; others allow more than one reading. None should be hidden or dismissed. They must also be read beside Jesus's direct statements that the Father is the only true God, greater than he is, and his own God. Islam concludes that later exalted language about Jesus should be read through his clear prophetic identity, not used to overturn the worship of God alone.

sections.title: Read the Strongest Verses With the Whole Record
sections.body: John 1:1, John 8:58, John 10:30, John 20:28, Philippians 2, Colossians 2:9, and Titus 2:13 form an important Christian case. Their grammar and context are debated in different ways. The larger question is whether they overturn Jesus's clear dependence on God or can be read within agency, Messiahship, and exaltation.

sections.title: Three Questions for Every Passage
sections.body: First, what does the wording most naturally mean in its immediate context? Second, does the passage identify Jesus with the one God or describe authority and honor granted by God? Third, how does the reading fit Jesus's prayers and statements of subordination? A doctrine should explain the complete pattern, not only its most favorable proof texts.

sections.title: John 1:1: The Word Was God
sections.body:
John opens by saying that the Word was with God and that the Word was God. The Greek wording commonly receives a qualitative sense: the Word has the nature or quality of God while remaining distinct from "the God" with whom the Word was.

This is a strong Christian text, but it is the narrator's theological prologue, not a sentence Jesus spoke. The same Gospel later records Jesus calling the Father "the only true God" and himself the one sent by Him (John 17:3). Muslims therefore read John 1:1 in light of biblical agency and wisdom language, while recognizing that "a god" is a weak minority translation.

sections.title: John 8:58: Before Abraham, 'I Am'
sections.body:
Jesus says, "Before Abraham was, I am." Mainstream Christian interpretation hears an echo of divine self-identification and a claim of preexistence. The wording is striking, and the attempt to stone Jesus shows that his opponents heard something offensive.

The Greek phrase ego eimi can also mean ordinary self-identification, as John 9:9 shows, so the words alone are not the unique divine name. The reaction of hostile opponents proves what they thought they heard, not that their interpretation was correct; John's Gospel repeatedly portrays misunderstanding. Even a claim to preexistence would require a further argument to prove equality with God. Muslims read the verse through Jesus's distinction between himself and the God who sent him.

sections.title: John 10:30: 'I and the Father Are One'
sections.body:
"I and the Father are one" occurs in a discussion of protecting Jesus's followers. Christians understand a unity of divine power and identity. Muslims note that the Greek word is neuter and does not mean one person, while John 17:21-23 uses closely related language when Jesus prays that the disciples may be one as he and the Father are one.

Jesus then cites Psalm 82:6, where human judges are called "gods," and describes himself as the one whom the Father sanctified and sent. The passage supports a uniquely authorized Messiah, but it does not force the conclusion that Jesus is the same God he calls Father.

sections.title: John 20:28: 'My Lord and My God'
sections.body:
Thomas addresses the risen Jesus as "My Lord and my God." Most scholars read both titles as directed to Jesus, and the exclamation-only reading is a minority position. This is therefore one of the strongest verses for the Christian case.

Yet the same chapter has Jesus say, "I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God" (John 20:17). John also applies elevated titles within a Jewish world where God's appointed agents could bear divine language without becoming the one God. Christians reconcile the texts through two natures. Muslims take Jesus's own statement that he has a God as the clearer guide to his identity.

sections.title: Philippians 2:6-8: Form, Equality, and Obedience
sections.body:
Philippians describes Christ in "the form of God," not exploiting or grasping equality with God, taking the form of a servant, and being obedient to death. Many scholars read this as a preexistent Christ choosing self-humbling. An influential minority reads it as an Adam comparison: unlike Adam, Jesus did not grasp at equality with God.

Either way, the passage distinguishes Christ from God and presents him as obedient. It is a hymn quoted or used by Paul, not a direct saying in which Jesus identifies himself as God. Islam recognizes the moral greatness of Jesus's obedience while denying that obedience to God is evidence of being God.

sections.title: Colossians 2:9: The Fullness of Deity
sections.body:
Colossians says that "all the fullness of deity" dwells bodily in Christ. Christians reasonably see this as very high Christology. Muslims note that Paul also prays for believers to be "filled with all the fullness of God" (Ephesians 3:19), so fullness language can describe God's presence and power without making its recipient God.

Colossians alone cannot decide whether the author means identity with God or the complete presence of God's gifts and authority in His Messiah. Jesus's own dependence and prayer remain part of the evidence.

sections.title: Titus 2:13: God and Savior
sections.body:
Most modern translations render Titus 2:13 as "our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ." The Greek construction strongly favors both titles referring to Jesus, although a minority has argued for two referents: God the Father and Jesus Christ.

This is significant evidence for the Christology of the Pastoral Epistles. It is not, however, a saying of Jesus. Many critical scholars also dispute Pauline authorship of Titus, while traditional Christians defend it. The verse shows that some early Christians used divine titles for Jesus; it does not erase the Gospel record of Jesus worshiping and being sent by God.

sections.title: The Quran's Clear Account of Jesus
sections.body:
The Quran resolves the tension by defining Jesus clearly. He is God's Messiah, word conveyed to Mary, spirit from Him, and messenger—not a person within God (Quran 4:171). His miraculous creation is compared with Adam's (Quran 3:59). He calls people to worship "my Lord and your Lord" (Quran 5:72), declares himself God's servant and prophet (Quran 19:30), and is described with Mary as eating food, a sign of creaturely dependence (Quran 5:75).

These verses do not alter Greek grammar. They provide the revealed framework in which Muslims read the New Testament: exalted titles honor God's Messiah, while the plain distinction between God and His messenger remains controlling.

sections.title: Jesus's Own Words About God
sections.body:
Jesus calls the Father "the only true God" (John 17:3), says "the Father is greater than I" (John 14:28), admits that the Son does not know the Hour (Mark 13:32), says he can do nothing by himself (John 5:30), and calls the Father "my God" after the resurrection (John 20:17).

Christian theology assigns these statements to Jesus's human nature while assigning divine titles to his divine nature. That framework is coherent within Nicene Christianity, but the Gospel verses themselves do not explain the distinction. Islam reads the direct statements as they stand: Jesus is a genuine human messenger who depends on God.

The choice is therefore not between respecting and ignoring Scripture. It is between a later two-natures synthesis and the simpler prophetic reading confirmed by the Quran.

sections.title: Exalted Language Is Not the Same as Identity
sections.body: The Bible can call judges 'gods' in a representative sense (Psalm 82:6; John 10:34–36), use divine titles for agents, and describe unity of purpose without numerical identity. This does not settle every verse, but it prevents the assumption that any elevated title automatically makes its bearer the Creator. Clear statements such as John 17:3 and 20:17 remain essential context.

sections.title: Why Tawhid Fits the Whole Pattern
sections.body: The divinity verses support a highly honored Messiah, especially when read through later Christian theology. Jesus's own worship provides the clearer interpretive center: he prays to God, is sent by God, receives authority from God, and calls the Father his God. Islam preserves all of that language without turning God's messenger into God.

sections.title: Focused Questions
sections.body:
**Does John 1:1 use the word God?** Yes, and its grammar is central to Christian interpretation; it still must be read with John's distinction between God and the Word.

**Does 'before Abraham was, I am' prove identity with Yahweh?** It expresses extraordinary preeminence, but the Greek phrase alone does not force the Exodus identification.

**Why did opponents seek to stone Jesus?** John records accusations of blasphemy, but an accusation is not proof that the accused accepted the charge.

**Which texts are clearest?** Jesus's direct prayers and statements about his God are less dependent on disputed grammar.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
Selected sources and further reading:

- **Jesus as God: The New Testament Use of Theos in Reference to Jesus** — Murray J. Harris. The standard technical, mainstream defense of reading theos as applied to Jesus in the New Testament, with detailed treatments of John 1:1, John 20:28, and Titus 2:13.
- **The Climax of the Covenant: Christ and the Law in Pauline Theology** — N. T. Wright. Collects Wright's influential 1986 essay on harpagmos and Philippians 2:5-11, the strongest modern statement of the kenotic, pre-existence reading.
- **Christology in the Making: A New Testament Inquiry into the Origins of the Doctrine of the Incarnation** — James D. G. Dunn. Presents the Adam-Christology reading of Philippians 2 and argues that New Testament belief in Jesus's pre-existence developed within, rather than from the start of, the earliest tradition.
- **The Doctrine of the Trinity: Christianity's Self-Inflicted Wound** — Anthony F. Buzzard and Charles F. Hunting.

faq.question: Which of the seven passages has the strongest grammatical case for calling Jesus God outright?
faq.answer: Among the seven, Titus 2:13 is generally regarded as grammatically the strongest single case, because the Granville Sharp construction — one article governing “God” and “Savior,” both joined to the name “Jesus Christ” — has been tested statistically against a wide body of Koine Greek and found to hold with high consistency wherever its conditions are met, according to Daniel B. Wallace’s research. Even here, a minority of scholars, following Ezra Abbot, continue to argue for a two-person reading.

faq.question: Is Colwell’s rule a reliable proof that John 1:1 calls Jesus “God” rather than “a god”?
faq.answer: Not by itself. E. C. Colwell’s 1933 study found that definite predicate nouns preceding the verb in Greek usually lack the article, but it describes nouns already known to be definite from context and does not independently establish that theos is definite in John 1:1c. Philip Harner’s 1973 study argued that most such nouns function qualitatively rather than definitely or indefinitely, a conclusion accepted broadly across the theological spectrum even though its theological implications remain disputed.

faq.question: Is the “I AM” of John 8:58 definitely a claim to be the God of Exodus 3:14?
faq.answer: Mainstream scholarship widely reads it that way, citing the parallel with the Septuagint’s egō eimi ho ōn and the crowd’s attempt to stone Jesus immediately afterward. Unitarian and Muslim scholars respond that egō eimi is ordinary Greek self-identification — used the same way by the healed blind man in John 9:9 — and propose that Jesus is claiming precedence in God’s plan rather than personal, literal pre-existence. Both readings are argued in the current literature, which is why the passage remains genuinely contested rather than settled by vocabulary alone.

faq.question: Does the Bible ever call Jesus God directly, in so many words?
faq.answer: John 1:1, John 20:28, Titus 2:13, and similar passages are commonly read that way, and some have a strong grammatical case within their authors' theology. The same Gospels also record Jesus calling the Father 'the only true God' (John 17:3), 'greater than I' (John 14:28), and 'my God' (John 20:17). Islam gives those direct sayings interpretive priority.

faq.question: Is the exclamation reading of John 20:28 as strong as the qualitative reading of John 1:1?
faq.answer: No. The qualitative reading of John 1:1 has broad support across the theological spectrum, although scholars disagree about its theological implications. Reading Thomas's words in John 20:28 as a mere exclamation is a minority view; most Johannine scholars understand both titles as addressed directly to Jesus.

faq.question: Does presenting both readings mean the question of Jesus’s divinity can’t be answered?
faq.answer: No. The texts can be weighed together. The Islamic conclusion is that Jesus's direct statements about the one God who sent him should govern the reading of later exalted titles, and that the Quran confirms this prophetic identity. Christian readers will disagree, but the evidence permits a clear, argued conclusion rather than permanent neutrality.
